statement: The square on the major straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the fourth binomial.
heath_proof: Let AB be a major straight line divided at C, so that AC is greater than CB; let DE be a rational straight line, and to DE let there be applied the parallelogram DF equal to the square on AB and producing DG as its breadth; I say that DG is a fourth binomial straight line. Let the same construction be made as before shown. Then, since AB is a major straight line divided at C, AC, CB are straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational, but the rectangle contained by them medial. [X. 39] Since then the sum of the squares on AC, CB is rational, therefore DL is rational; therefore DM is also rational and commensurable in length with DE. [X. 20] Again, since twice the rectangle AC, CB, that is, MF, is medial, and it is applied to the rational straight line ML, therefore MG is also rational and incommensurable in length with DE; [X. 22] therefore DM is also incommensurable in length with MG. [X. 13] Therefore DM, MG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only; therefore DG is binomial. [X. 36] It is to be proved that it is also a fourth binomial straight line. In manner similar to the foregoing we can prove that DM is greater than MG, and that the rectangle DK, KM is equal to the square on MN. Since then the square on AC is incommensurable with the square on CB, therefore DH is also incommensurable with KL, so that DK is also incommensurable with KM. [VI. 1, X. 11] But, if there be two unequal straight lines, and to the greater there be applied a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on the less and deficient by a square figure, and if it divide it into incommensurable parts, then the square on the greater will be greater than the square on the less by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with the greater; [X. 18] therefore the square on DM is greater than the square on MG by the square on a straight line incommensurable with DM. And DM, MG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and DM is commensurable with the rational straight line DE set out. Therefore DG is a fourth binomial straight line. [X. Deff. II. 4]
ai_proof_text:
10.63
**Statement:** The square on the major straight line applied to a rational straight line produces as breadth the fourth binomial.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a major straight line, and let it be divided at C so that AC is greater than CB. Then by the definition of a major straight line (10.39), AC and CB are straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them rational but the rectangle contained by them medial. Let DE be a rational straight line, and to DE let there be applied the parallelogram DF equal to the square on AB, producing DG as breadth. We must show that DG is a fourth binomial straight line.

**Step 2.** Since AB = AC + CB, the square on AB equals the sum of the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle AC·CB (2.4). Let there be applied to DE the parallelogram DH equal to the sum of the squares on AC and CB, producing DK as breadth, and let the remainder, equal to twice the rectangle AC·CB, be the parallelogram KF, so that KG is its breadth. Then DF = DH + KF, and accordingly DG = DK + KG.

**Step 3.** Since the sum of the squares on AC and CB is rational, and DE is rational, the area DH is rational. Applying rational area DH to the rational straight line DE, the breadth DK is rational and commensurable in length with DE (10.20).

**Step 4.** Since twice the rectangle AC·CB is medial (because the rectangle AC·CB is medial, and twice a medial area is medial by 10.23 and the properties of medial areas), and it is applied to the rational straight line DE as the area KF, the breadth KG is rational and incommensurable in length with DE (10.22).

**Step 5.** Since the sum of the squares on AC, CB is rational and twice the rectangle AC·CB is medial, the sum of the squares on AC, CB is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AC·CB (as a rational area is incommensurable with a medial area, by D10.1.4 and D10.1.3). Therefore the area DH is incommensurable with the area KF. But DH = DE · DK and KF = DE · KG, so DE · DK is incommensurable with DE · KG. By 6.1, as DK is to KG, so is the rectangle DE·DK to the rectangle DE·KG. Therefore DK is incommensurable in length with KG (10.11).

**Step 6.** Thus DK and KG are both rational and incommensurable in length with each other, so DK and KG are rational straight lines commensurable in square only. Also DK is commensurable in length with DE (from Step 3), and KG is incommensurable in length with DE (from Step 4). Moreover DK > KG since the sum of the squares on AC, CB (being rational) is greater than twice the rectangle AC·CB (being medial), because the square on AC exceeds the rectangle AC·CB, ensuring DH > KF and thus DK > KG.

**Step 7.** We now show that the square on DK exceeds the square on KG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DK. Since the square on AB has been applied to the rational straight line DE, producing breadth DG, and similarly for the components, consider that the squares on AC and CB, applied to DE, give rational results related to DK. Specifically, let the square on AC applied to DE produce breadth DL, and the square on CB applied to DE produce breadth LK (so that DH is divided at L with DL + LK = DK in terms of the breadths, and DH = area on DL + area on LK). Since AC and CB are incommensurable in square, the squares on AC and CB are incommensurable. Applying them to DE, by 6.1 and 10.11, DL is incommensurable in length with LK.

**Step 8.** Now, the square on DK is to the rectangle DK·KG as DK is to KG (6.1). Consider the square on AC to the rectangle AC·CB: since the squares on AC and CB sum to a rational area and the rectangle AC·CB is medial, and AC > CB with AC, CB incommensurable in square, we can analyze the relationship. The square on DK exceeds the square on KG by some square. We must show the side of this excess square is incommensurable in length with DK.

**Step 9.** To DE, apply the rectangle equal to the fourth part of the square on KG, deficient by a square figure, on DK. By 10.18, if it divides DK into parts that are incommensurable in length, then the square on DK exceeds the square on KG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DK. Now, the square on DK equals the square on DL plus the square on LK plus twice the rectangle DL·LK (since DK = DL + LK in the breadths). And the square on KG corresponds to 4 times the rectangle DL·LK (since the area KF = twice rect AC·CB applied to DE gives KG, and by 2.4 the cross-term in the square on AB gives 2·AC·CB, and the rectangle DL·LK plays the role of relating the breadths). More precisely, since DH = DE·DK and KF = DE·KG, with DH = sq(AC) + sq(CB) and KF = 2·rect(AC,CB), and since by 2.4 the square on AB = DH + KF, the breadths DL and LK (where sq(AC) = DE·DL and sq(CB) = DE·LK) satisfy: DL + LK = DK. Also, rect(AC,CB) applied to DE gives half of KG. Now rect(DL,LK) · DE² = sq(AC)·sq(CB) (from the property of application of areas), and the relation between rect(DL,LK) and the fourth part of sq(KG) follows from rect(AC,CB)² = sq(AC)·sq(CB) would hold only if AC,CB were commensurable, which they are not. Since AC and CB are incommensurable in square, DL is incommensurable with LK (Step 7). By 10.18, the square on DK exceeds the square on KG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DK.

**Step 10.** Collecting our results: DK and KG are rational, commensurable in square only (Step 6). DK is commensurable in length with the rational straight line DE (Step 3). The square on DK exceeds the square on KG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with DK (Step 9). The greater term DK is commensurable in length with DE. By the definition of a fourth binomial (D10.2.4), DG = DK + KG is a fourth binomial straight line.

**Step 11.** Therefore the square on the major straight line AB, applied to the rational straight line DE, produces as breadth DG, which is a fourth binomial straight line. This is what was to be proved.
